title: MPG (US) vs MPG (UK) vs L/100 km — EPA and WLTP Converted
h1: Fuel economy — MPG US, MPG UK, and L/100 km reconciled
description: 30 MPG US = 36 MPG UK = 7.84 L/100 km. Same car, three sticker numbers. Plus why EPA and WLTP disagree by 15%.

hero: A 30 MPG US car is 36 MPG UK and 7.84 L/100 km — same fuel consumption, three number systems. The US gallon is smaller than the UK gallon by 20%; L/100 km inverts the metric so the number grows as efficiency drops.
body: Three habits collide in car reviews: American MPG (US gallon), British MPG (Imperial gallon), and metric L/100 km. The gallons differ, and the L/100 km scale runs inverse to MPG — halving the L/100 km number doubles efficiency, whereas doubling MPG doubles it too but in the other direction. Cross-comparing without conversion is where most car forums argue past each other.
## The exact factors

> 1 US gallon = 3.7854 L
> 1 Imperial gallon = 4.5461 L (20% larger)
> 1 Imp gal = 1.20095 US gal
> Conversion: MPG US → L/100 km = 235.215 / MPG_US
> MPG UK → L/100 km = 282.481 / MPG_UK
> MPG US → MPG UK = MPG_US × 1.20095

## Why EPA and WLTP disagree

The EPA (US) tests on the FTP-75 city cycle and HWFET highway cycle, at 20°C ambient, no accessories. WLTP (EU/UK from 2018) uses four phases (low/medium/high/extra-high) with realistic acceleration and topping 131 km/h. Same car:

**Toyota Corolla Hybrid 2024.** EPA combined: 50 MPG US. WLTP combined: 4.4 L/100 km = 53 MPG US equivalent. Close — the EPA number happens to align with WLTP on hybrids. For pure ICE cars, WLTP typically reads 10–15% worse than EPA (higher fuel use) because of the realistic accessory load and higher top speeds.
**BMW 320i.** EPA 30 MPG combined. WLTP 6.9 L/100 km = 34 MPG US equivalent — 13% better on paper. Same car, same driving, different test protocol.
## Real-world vs sticker
Fuelly.com and Spritmonitor.de publish crowdsourced real-world numbers. Median gap versus sticker:
- EPA combined: real world runs 5–10% worse than sticker.
- WLTP combined: real world runs 8–20% worse.
- NEDC (pre-2018 Europe): real world runs 30–40% worse — this is why the EU replaced it.
The pattern: newer, more realistic test cycles narrow the gap. WLTP is not yet as accurate as EPA but is closing.
## Worked example — cross-shopping US and EU cars

You are comparing a US-market Honda Civic '32 MPG combined EPA' against an EU-market VW Golf '5.9 L/100 km WLTP'. Convert Civic: 32 MPG US → 235.215/32 = 7.35 L/100 km. Now compare on the same scale: Civic 7.35 vs Golf 5.9 — Golf is 20% more efficient on paper. Real-world adjust: Civic 7.7 (EPA -5%), Golf 6.8 (WLTP -15%) — Golf still wins but only 12%, not 20%.
## Diesel vs petrol accounting

Diesel has 13% higher volumetric energy density than petrol. A diesel returning 6.0 L/100 km uses the same energy as a petrol at 6.8 L/100 km. Cost-per-km depends on local pump prices; energy-per-km is what physics cares about. Some EU consumer guides now list 'petrol-equivalent L/100 km' for diesels to make the comparison fair.
## EV efficiency — MPGe and kWh/100 mi

EVs are labelled MPGe (miles per gallon equivalent) using 33.7 kWh = 1 gallon of petrol by energy content. Tesla Model 3 rated 133 MPGe = 25 kWh/100 mi = 15.5 kWh/100 km. To compare fuel cost: US petrol at $3.50/gal and electricity at $0.15/kWh, a 30 MPG petrol car costs $0.117/mi; a 133 MPGe EV costs $0.038/mi. 3× cheaper per mile at the pump, ignoring capital cost.
## The five-second recap

Convert MPG US to L/100 km: divide 235 by MPG. UK gallon is 20% bigger, so MPG UK = MPG US × 1.20. WLTP reads worse than EPA on ICE cars, similar on hybrids. Real world is 5–15% worse than any sticker.

faqs.q: Why is the UK MPG number bigger for the same car?
faqs.a: The Imperial gallon is 4.546 L versus the US gallon's 3.785 L — 20% larger. A car goes further on 'one gallon' when the gallon is bigger, so the number reads higher without any efficiency change.

faqs.q: Is L/100 km a better metric than MPG?
faqs.a: For comparing consumption directly, yes — the number scales linearly with fuel burnt. MPG is a rate, so improvements from 15→20 MPG save far more fuel than 40→45 MPG despite looking equal on the dial.
EPA defines 1 gallon of petrol as 33.7 kWh by lower heating value. MPGe = miles per 33.7 kWh. Useful for comparing EV to ICE at a first glance; not a direct cost comparison.
Same cycle, but the battery has to end at the same state of charge — hybrids cannot cheat by depleting the battery over the test. Plug-in hybrids get a separate 'utility factor' weighted average.

faqs.q: Do winter numbers really drop that much?
faqs.a: Yes. Cold starts, denser air, winter tire drag, and cabin heater all knock 10–30% off MPG for the first 10 minutes. Short winter trips barely warm the engine — average dips 15–25% November–February in cold climates.
